content: Lamivudine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) are indicated for use in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. The recommended dosage is one tablet containing lamivudine 300 mg and tenofovir 300 mg, taken orally once daily in combination with other antiretroviral therapies (ARTs). This combination is approved for use in adults and children weighing more than 35 kg. The regimen includes two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), lamivudine and tenofovir. Clinical trials have not included sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 years or older to determine if they respond differently from younger individuals. Caution is advised when administering lamivudine to elderly patients due to the increased likelihood of decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies. The co-administration of lamivudine with certain drugs, such as emtricitabine-containing products, is contraindicated due to the risk of therapeutic duplication and increased risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Similarly, lamivudine should not be used with elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir, as this combination is a complete regimen for HIV and should not be combined with other antiretrovirals. Additionally, antiretroviral medications may interfere with the manufacturing of certain cell-based therapies, such as atidarsagene autotemcel, betibeglogene autotemcel, and lovotibeglogene autotemcel. Patients should discontinue ARTs at least one month before cell mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed. Certain drug interactions may alter the efficacy or toxicity of lamivudine. Tafenoquine, an inhibitor of organic cation transporter-2 (OCT2) and multidrug and toxin extrusion (MATE) transporters, may increase lamivudine levels, necessitating close monitoring for toxicity. Similarly, trilaciclib, an OCT2 and MATE inhibitor, may reduce lamivudine levels, and co-administration should be avoided. Drugs like trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole can increase lamivudine levels by reducing renal clearance, while others, such as orlistat, may decrease its absorption, potentially leading to loss of virologic control. Lamivudine and tenofovir DF both carry a risk of immune reconstitution syndrome, which may manifest as an inflammatory response to residual opportunistic infections during the initial phase of combination ART. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves' disease or Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported in this setting, with variable onset times. Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients co-infected with HBV and HIV-1 who discontinue lamivudine or tenofovir DF. These patients require close hepatic monitoring and initiation of anti-hepatitis B treatment if necessary. Lamivudine should be used cautiously in pediatric patients with a history of pancreatitis or significant risk factors for its development. In pregnant women, lamivudine has shown embryonic toxicity in animal studies, but its relevance to human pregnancy is unclear. Tenofovir DF should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed, and breastfeeding is not recommended for HIV-1-infected mothers due to the risk of postnatal transmission, viral resistance, and adverse reactions in infants. Adverse reactions to lamivudine and tenofovir DF include rash (18%), headache (14%), pain (13%), diarrhea (11%), depression (11%), back pain (9%), fever (8%), abdominal pain (7%), asthenia (6%), anxiety (6%), arthralgia (5%), insomnia (5%), pneumonia (5%), myalgia (3%), dizziness (3%), lipodystrophy (1%), and peripheral neuropathy (1%). Severe cases of lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatalities, have been reported with nucleoside analogs and other ARTs. Treatment should be suspended in patients who develop clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity. Triple NRTI regimens are generally less effective than regimens containing two NRTIs combined with a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor or a protease inhibitor. Early virologic failure and high rates of resistance substitutions have been reported with triple NRTI regimens, and their use should be approached with caution. Lamivudine and tenofovir DF are not approved for chronic hepatitis B treatment, and their safety and efficacy in HBV/HIV-1 co-infected patients have not been established. If used inappropriately as monotherapy for HIV-1, rapid emergence of resistance is likely. Patients receiving combination ART may experience body fat redistribution or accumulation, such as central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, or a cushingoid appearance. An ART pregnancy registry is available to monitor outcomes in pregnant women exposed to these medications.
